vote_result: 9-3 hold (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan dissented hawkish, preferring a 25bp hike)
stance_summary: The FOMC has entered its most contested policy juncture in years, with Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole remarks pushing rate-hike odds for the September 15-16 meeting to roughly 56-58% on CME FedWatch, up sharply from about one-in-three a month earlier. Three regional presidents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) already dissented hawkishly in July, and Governors Barr and Cook have since signaled openness to a hike, while Waller and Bowman argue for patience given signs of disinflation.
policy_outlook: The August CPI report due September 11 is widely viewed as the decisive input before the meeting, with several voters (Waller, Barr, Williams) explicitly conditioning their votes on that data. A quarter-point hike to 3.75-4.00% is now roughly a coin flip with markets, while a hold would likely come with hawkish guidance given persistent above-target inflation (headline CPI 3.4% y/y, PCE near 3.7% y/y) despite a still-solid labor market (4.1% unemployment, +162k payrolls in August).
alert: August CPI (Sept 11) is pivotal ahead of the Sept 15-16 decision; FedWatch-implied hike odds have swung between ~34% and ~70% over the past month, making this the most closely contested meeting since the three-way hawkish dissent of September 2016.

members.name: Kevin Warsh
members.title: Chairman
members.note: In his first Jackson Hole address as Chair, Warsh said he was 'impressed' by the economy's strength but warned that softer monthly inflation readings 'do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.' He continues to withhold explicit forward guidance, but markets read his tone as tilting toward a September hike.
members.latest_source: Keynote remarks, Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, August 28, 2026

members.name: Jerome Powell
members.title: Governor (former Chair)
members.note: Powell stepped down as Chair in May 2026 but chose to remain on the Board of Governors, citing ongoing legal disputes over the Fed's independence. He has kept a deliberately low public profile on rate policy since Warsh took over, avoiding direct commentary on the September decision.
members.latest_source: Final press conference as Chair, April 29, 2026

members.name: John Williams
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York; Vice Chair of the FOMC
members.note: Williams shifted from a hold-leaning stance to openness on a September hike, saying 'there's no clear signs right now whether monetary policy currently is sufficient' to return inflation to target. He called recent inflation data 'encouraging' but wants a fuller picture before committing.

members.name: Michael Barr
members.title: Governor
members.note: Barr said he is watching the risk of 'broader price pressures taking hold' after more than five years of above-target inflation, and would support acting 'decisively to raise rates' if August data doesn't show moderation. He remains data-dependent heading into the meeting.
members.latest_source: Speech at the Second Chance Lending Forum, September 1, 2026

members.name: Michelle Bowman
members.title: Vice Chair for Supervision; Governor
members.note: Bowman has cautioned against hiking in response to what she views as temporary, supply-driven energy price spikes, warning that 'reacting to temporarily elevated energy price inflation would add unwarranted policy restraint.' She has generally favored holding or easing over the past year.
members.latest_source: Speech at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, May 29, 2026

members.name: Lisa Cook
members.title: Governor
members.note: Cook says she views inflation risk as greater than employment risk right now and is 'prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary' if disinflation doesn't continue. She voted for the July hold but flagged the risk that persistent above-target inflation becomes entrenched in wage- and price-setting.
members.latest_source: Speech to the Anchorage Economic Development Corporation, August 5, 2026

members.name: Philip Jefferson
members.title: Vice Chair; Governor
members.note: Jefferson says he is 'firmly committed' to the 2% target and has 'not prejudged' the September meeting, but acknowledged it 'could be appropriate to reconsider our current policy stance' if inflation doesn't cool soon. He frames the decision as a genuine balancing act between mandate goals.
members.latest_source: Speech on navigating economic shocks, July 16, 2026

members.name: Christopher Waller
members.title: Governor
members.note: Waller said he is 'inclined to support holding' rates steady given recent signs of disinflation, but conceded 'if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.' His comments diverged notably from Warsh's more hawkish Jackson Hole tone.

members.name: Beth Hammack
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland
members.dissent_detail: Dissented at the July 2026 meeting, preferring an immediate 25bp hike; said policy 'isn't restrictive enough' and cited demand-side as well as supply-side inflation pressure.
members.note: Hammack has argued 'now is the time for the [FOMC] to act to speed the return of PCE inflation to our 2 percent objective.' She continues to see inflation risks as demand-driven and not just a temporary energy shock.
members.latest_source: Statement following the July 29, 2026 FOMC decision

members.name: Neel Kashkari
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis
members.dissent_detail: Dissented in July for a 25bp hike, arguing 'a potential series of small policy moves would be better than waiting' for larger action later.
members.note: Kashkari has pointed to strong corporate earnings, a resilient consumer, and persistent supply shocks (tariffs, AI-related capex, energy) as evidence that policy isn't restrictive enough. He says the chairman has given him 'full latitude' to dissent.

members.name: Lorie Logan
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
members.dissent_detail: Dissented in July for a 25bp hike, the most explicit of the three dissenters in saying rates should be 'modestly' higher.
members.note: Logan has argued the Fed 'can't count on an unexpected jolt to the economy' to bring inflation down and needs to act proactively rather than wait. She remains the most consistently hawkish voice on the current committee.
members.latest_source: Statement following the July 29, 2026 FOMC decision

members.name: Anna Paulson
members.title: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia
members.note: Paulson voted with the July hold majority, calling it 'not a close call,' while describing current policy as only 'mildly restrictive' — a framing some read as leaving room to support tightening if inflation data disappoint. She has since been characterized as prepared to back a hike if core inflation fails to show sustained cooling.
